READ THIS FIRSTThe whole course in six sentences

If you remember nothing else
  1. A wire stops being a wire and becomes a transmission line when it is long compared to a wavelength. Then voltage depends on where you are, not just when.
  2. Modelling the line as infinitely many tiny – sections gives the telegrapher's equations, which combine into the 1-D wave equation. Signals travel at .
  3. For a wave going one way, the line forces a fixed ratio : the characteristic impedance.
  4. A load cannot satisfy that ratio, so a reflected wave is born: . This single formula is 50% of the course.
  5. Forward + reflected waves interfere ⇒ standing waves, maxima and minima every , measured by VSWR.
  6. Looking into the line from distance , you see a transformed impedance . A line inverts normalised impedance; a line repeats it. That is where all the tricks come from.

Not sure what “the wave” even refers to? Start at Ground Floor below — it builds the picture from ordinary circuit theory, with diagrams, before any formula appears.

Everything below expands those six points. Boxes marked INTUITION are for understanding, DERIVATION for the algebra you may be asked to reproduce, EXAM for what actually gets asked.

GROUND FLOOR — START HEREWhat "the wave" actually is

If the word "wave" in this course feels like it arrived from nowhere, that is because it did. Nobody tells you the one thing that has to change in your head first. Here it is, slowly.

Step 1 — what you currently believe about a wire

In every circuits course you have taken, a wire has one voltage. Touch a probe anywhere along it and you read the same number. If the battery says 5 V, the whole wire is at 5 V — instantly, everywhere.

This is a very good approximation. It is also, strictly speaking, false.

Step 2 — the one physical fact that breaks it

Electricity is not instant. When you close a switch, the "news" that the voltage has changed travels down the wire at a finite speed — typically around m/s, about two-thirds the speed of light. Fast, but not infinite.

So picture a long wire and a switch closing at . Take a photograph of the whole wire at three different moments:

This is the whole idea

Look at the middle row. At that single instant, the left half of the wire is at 5 V and the right half is at 0 V.

Two points on one continuous piece of copper, at the same moment, holding different voltages. Circuit theory says that cannot happen. It happens.

The moment voltage depends on where you are as well as when, you are no longer doing circuit theory. You are doing wave theory. That is the entire reason this course exists.

Step 3 — now wiggle the source instead of switching it once

A step gives you one travelling edge. Now suppose the source is a sine generator, oscillating up and down forever. It keeps launching new "news" down the wire, continuously.

The result is that the voltage-versus-position picture stops being a single step and becomes a repeating ripple, sliding along the wire. That ripple is "the wave."

Step 4 — the graph you have never drawn before

Here is where most of the confusion lives. There are two completely different graphs you can draw, and they look identical, and they mean opposite things.

Read the difference carefully

Graph A ( against ). Pick one point on the wire. Stand there. Watch the voltage go up and down as time passes. This is what an oscilloscope shows you, and it is the only graph you have ever drawn. The repeat distance is a period , measured in seconds.

Graph B ( against ). Freeze time. Photograph the entire wire at one instant. Plot the voltage you find at every position. The repeat distance is a wavelength , measured in metres.

When this course says "the wave," it means Graph B — a shape laid out in space, along the wire. Everything that follows — wavelength, standing waves, "a quarter-wave line" — is about that spatial shape. If you keep picturing Graph A, none of it will make sense, because none of it is about time.

The two are linked by the speed: in one period the pattern slides forward by exactly one wavelength, so .

Step 5 — so when does any of this matter?

You now have two lengths in metres that you can compare directly:

  • — the distance over which the voltage pattern completes one full wiggle.
  • — the length of your actual wire.

Lay the wire against the wave and look:

The punchline

If your wire is short compared to , it only ever sits on a tiny, nearly flat piece of the wave. Both ends read the same voltage. Circuit theory is fine. We call this lumped.

If your wire is comparable to or longer, a whole wiggle fits on it. One end can be at  V while a point halfway along is at  V. We call this distributed, and everything in Sections 1–19 follows.

The number that measures "short or long compared to " is the ratio — and dressed up in radians, that is exactly the you meet in the next section. Nothing more.

The two habits to break
  1. "A wire has one voltage." It does not. It has a voltage profile — a different number at every point.
  2. "A wave means something moving up and down in time." Here it means a shape spread out along the wire. Time makes that shape slide; it is not what makes it a wave.

SECTION 0Why any of this exists

In circuit theory you were told a wire is a wire: the same voltage appears at both ends, instantly. That is a lie that stops working at high frequency.

A lumped circuit assumes a signal change propagates across the whole circuit instantaneously. Your resistor "knows" immediately what the source did. That is fine when the physical size of the circuit is much smaller than the wavelength of the signal.

A distributed circuit (a transmission line) is one where that assumption fails: the signal takes real time to travel, so and are functions of both position and time — written , .

The criterion

Signals travel at speed . In one period a wave covers one wavelength, . The question is how that wavelength compares to the length of your line, . The number that measures it is called the electrical length:

Where does come from?

It is a unit conversion, not a physical law. Build it in two steps.

Step 1 — what is. is a rate: the number of radians of phase the wave picks up per metre travelled. Units: rad/m.

Step 2 — pin the rate down. By definition, one wavelength is one complete cycle of the wave, and one complete cycle is radians. So:

Divide both sides by to get radians per metre:

That is the entire derivation. Then is just rate distance — the same structure as :

Intuition — what the number is telling you

Look at the middle of that fraction. The piece is simply how many wavelengths fit onto your line. The only converts that count into radians.

So answers one question: how much of a wave is sitting on the line at any instant?

  • → rad. Both ends of the line are at essentially the same point in the wave's cycle, so the voltage is the same everywhere. Ordinary circuit theory works.
  • → . A whole wave fits on the line: one end can be at a peak while the other sits at a trough. Circuit theory is dead.

The single sentence worth memorising:

is the phase difference, in radians, between the two ends of the line.

This is also why it is called electrical length. The length in metres means nothing by itself — only the length relative to the wavelength matters. The same 10 cm wire is electrically invisible at 1 kHz and electrically enormous at 1 GHz, and is the one number that tells the two situations apart.

Worked check — the same wire at two frequencies

Take m/s and a cm m trace.

At GHz:

Exactly one wavelength sits on the line. Firmly distributed.

At kHz:

Utterly negligible. Lumped. Same piece of copper, opposite conclusions.

Hence the rule:

  •  () → delay is negligible → treat as lumped.
  • or bigger → must use transmission line theory.

Your notes make this concrete with m/s:

FrequencyWavelength Does a 10 cm PCB trace matter?
1 kHz100 kmNo. . Lumped.
1 MHz100 mBarely. .
1 GHz10 cmYes. . Full wave behaviour.
Intuition

It is not "high frequency" that matters — it is length measured in wavelengths. A 1 kHz signal on a 200 km undersea cable is absolutely a transmission line problem. A 1 GHz signal across a 1 mm chip is not. This is why the theory was invented for telegraph cables (hence "telegrapher's equations") long before radio.

THE TOOLKIT — BUILD THIS FIRSTThe five things the rest of the course assumes

From here on, every page uses five ideas without stopping to explain them: inductance, capacitance, KVL/KCL, phasors, and impedance. If any of those are shaky, the maths later will look like magic. So here they are, slowly, from the bottom.

How to use this section

T1, T2, T3 you need before Section 1. T4 and T5 you only need from Section 7 onward — you can skip them on a first pass and come back.

T1 — Inductance: why a plain wire fights you

Start with a fact from physics: a current creates a magnetic field around it. Not just in a coil — any current, in any wire, at all times. The field wraps around the wire in circles.

That field holds energy. To make the field bigger you must put energy in; when it shrinks, you get energy back. So changing the current is not free — and the circuit experiences that cost as a voltage appearing across the wire.

The relationship turns out to be beautifully simple:

Read that equation in words

The voltage across an inductor does not depend on how much current is flowing. It depends on how fast the current is changing. That is what means: the rate of change of .

Big steady current, not changing? Zero volts. Tiny current that flips direction very fast? Possibly enormous volts.

Why this matters for us

Two consequences you will use constantly:

  • At DC, an inductor is invisible. constant ⇒ ⇒ . It behaves as a plain piece of wire. This is why nobody mentioned inductance in your DC circuits course.
  • At high frequency, it dominates. A sinusoid at frequency changes faster as rises, so grows, so the voltage grows. The higher the frequency, the more the wire fights.

That single asymmetry — harmless at DC, brutal at GHz — is half the reason this entire course exists.

You do not need a coil. A straight wire has inductance simply because current flows through it. For coaxial cable it is roughly 250 nH per metre. We write it as per unit length, units H/m.

T2 — Capacitance: why two wires near each other store charge

Take any two conductors separated by a gap. Push charge onto one; an equal and opposite charge is attracted onto the other. Charge is now stored, and a voltage appears between them.

Getting to the equation

The stored charge is proportional to the voltage: . The constant is the capacitance — how much charge you get per volt.

Current is, by definition, the rate at which charge moves: .

Substitute and differentiate:

The pattern — and the mirror image

Compare the two equations you now have. They are mirror images:

  • Inductor: . Resists change in current. Short circuit at DC.
  • Capacitor: . Resists change in voltage. Open circuit at DC.

Swap and and one becomes the other. This symmetry runs through the whole course — you will meet it again as and .

Again, no component needed: any two wires running alongside each other are a capacitor. Coax is about 100 pF per metre. We write per unit length, units F/m.

Where this is going

A transmission line is two conductors running side by side. So it automatically, unavoidably has both: inductance along it, and capacitance across it. Not because someone added components — because of what it physically is. Section 1 does nothing more than take that seriously.

T3 — KVL and KCL: the only two circuit laws we use

Why they are true

KVL (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law). Voltage is like height on a hill. Walk any closed loop and you must return to the height you started at, so all the rises and drops cancel. Going round a circuit loop, the voltages sum to zero.

KCL (Kirchhoff's Current Law). Charge is not created or destroyed and does not pile up at a junction. So the current arriving equals the current leaving.

How we will use them

In Section 1 we chop the line into slices of length and apply exactly these two laws to one slice:

  • KVL across the slice, through the series inductance → tells us how voltage changes with position.
  • KCL at the node, with current leaking into the shunt capacitance → tells us how current changes with position.

Those two statements are the telegrapher's equations. Nothing more sophisticated is involved.

T4 — Phasors: why complex numbers turn up in a circuits course

This is the part that looks like it came from nowhere. It did not. It is a labour-saving trick, and here is the labour it saves.

The problem

Once the source is a sinusoid, every voltage and current in the circuit is of the form . To add two of them, or differentiate them, you need trigonometric identities, and it becomes miserable fast. We want something better.

Step 1: what actually is

— but do not think of it as a "number that does not exist." Think of it as an instruction: rotate by 90°.

Draw numbers as arrows from the origin. The number is an arrow pointing right. Multiply by and it rotates a quarter turn, to point up. Multiply by again and it points left — which is . And indeed . The algebra and the geometry agree.

Step 2: Euler's formula

Do not panic at this. It says one thing: is an arrow of length 1, pointing at angle . Its horizontal shadow is , its vertical shadow is . That is the whole content.

Step 3: let the angle grow with time

Now put . As increases, the angle increases, so is an arrow spinning steadily anticlockwise, at radians per second.

The idea in one line

A sine wave is the shadow of something going round in a circle. So instead of tracking a wiggly curve through time, track the arrow. The arrow has just two numbers — length (the amplitude) and angle (the phase) — and they do not change with time.

Writing it down properly

Take our sinusoid and pull it apart:

The spinning part is the same for everything in the circuit — every voltage and current oscillates at the source frequency. So it carries no useful information, and we simply stop writing it.

What is left, , is the phasor: one complex number holding the amplitude and the phase. To recover the real signal, multiply by and take the real part.

Step 4: the payoff — calculus becomes multiplication

The one line that justifies the entire method

Differentiate the spinning arrow:

Differentiating gave back the same thing, times . So in phasor world:

Why this is such a big deal

Differential equations become ordinary algebra. That is the whole reason for the detour through complex numbers — not elegance, laziness. Every in the telegrapher's equations becomes a , and a partial differential equation collapses into something you can solve with GCSE algebra.

The geometric reason it works: differentiating a cosine gives a negative sine, which is the same wave shifted by 90°. And multiplying by is rotating by 90°. The calculus and the rotation are the same operation.

T5 — Impedance: Ohm's law for things that are not resistors

Now feed each component its phasor and see what comes out as.

Derivation — all three components

Resistor. , no derivatives, nothing changes:

Inductor. . Replace with :

Capacitor. , so :

In every case the ratio is a single (complex) number. We call it the impedance , and now one law covers everything:

What the real and imaginary parts mean physically

Real part — dissipation. Energy goes in and does not come back; it leaves as heat. Only resistance does this.

Imaginary part — storage. Energy is borrowed for part of the cycle and handed back later. Nothing is lost. This is called reactance, written , and .

Sign of the imaginary part: is inductive (voltage leads current), is capacitive (current leads voltage).

Notice both reactances depend on : the inductor's grows with frequency, the capacitor's shrinks. Change the frequency and the whole circuit behaves differently — which is exactly why a wire that is fine at 1 kHz misbehaves at 1 GHz.

Why you should care, specifically

Nearly every result in the rest of this course is a statement about impedance:

  • — the impedance a line demands.
  • — reflections happen when two impedances disagree.
  • — the line transforms one impedance into another.
  • A shorted stub gives — purely imaginary, so purely storage, so a piece of wire has become an inductor or a capacitor.

If "impedance" means something concrete to you, those all read as sentences rather than symbols.

Checklist before Section 1
  1. An inductor's voltage depends on the rate of change of current: .
  2. A capacitor's current depends on the rate of change of voltage: .
  3. Any two conductors side by side have both, per metre, automatically.
  4. KVL: voltages round a loop sum to zero. KCL: current in = current out.
  5. A phasor is a static arrow: length = amplitude, angle = phase. becomes .
  6. Impedance is : real part burns energy, imaginary part stores it.

SECTION 1The distributed model & telegrapher's equations

Take any two parallel conductors (coaxial cable, two metal strips, twisted pair). Two facts of electromagnetism:

  • Current flowing along them creates magnetic flux → there is inductance per unit length (H/m).
  • A voltage difference between them stores charge → there is capacitance per unit length (F/m).

So model a short slice of length as a series inductor and a shunt capacitor , and chain infinitely many of them.

Derivation — the two telegrapher's equations

KVL around one slice. The voltage dropped across the series inductor is :

Divide by and let . The left side is :

KCL at one node. Whatever current does not continue forward must charge the shunt capacitor:

Intuition

Read them in words: (1) voltage falls along the line because current is changing — series inductance resists changes in current. (2) current falls along the line because voltage is changing — some current is being diverted to charge the shunt capacitance.

They are coupled: a change in makes a change in , which makes a change in further along… That chain reaction is the propagating wave. It is exactly the same mathematics as a mass-on-springs chain, or a rope: inertia () trading energy with a restoring element ().

SECTION 3Characteristic impedance

The single most important idea in the course: for a wave travelling one way, the line dictates a fixed ratio between voltage and current.

Derivation — forward wave

Assume a purely forward wave. Voltage and current must have the same shape (both obey the same wave equation and are coupled by (1)):

Substitute into telegrapher's equation (1), :

Cancel (true for all , so the coefficients must match):

Backward wave. Repeat with , so and the LHS flips sign:

Where the minus sign comes from — students lose marks here

It is not that the backward wave has negative impedance. It is a bookkeeping convention: we define positive current as flowing in the direction, for both waves. The backward wave carries power in the direction, so with our fixed sign convention its current comes out negative relative to its voltage. Power then correctly comes out negative (flowing backward).

Hence the total fields on a line are always written:

— note the plus in , minus in . Nearly every derivation in this course starts from these two lines.

Intuition — is not a resistor

An infinitely long line draws current from a source and never gives it back — so it behaves like a resistor of ohms. But no energy is dissipated as heat. The energy is carried away down the line forever. is a property of geometry and materials only (it is , and come from the cross-section) — it does not depend on length, frequency (for a lossless line), or what you connect.

Think of it as the line's "personality": the exchange rate between volts and amps that this particular pipe insists on. 50 Ω and 75 Ω coax are the industry-standard personalities.

Note also and are the two independent combinations of and — between them they contain everything about a lossless line.

Exam

The key insight

SECTION 5Reflection at the load —

The pulse arrives at the load carrying the ratio . But the load demands . If , both cannot be satisfied — unless a second, backward wave appears. That is a reflection.

Derivation — the reflection coefficient

At the load, total voltage and total current are the sums of both waves:

Solve for : :

Read every case off that one formula

LoadWhat happens physically
 matchedNo reflection at all. Load absorbs 100% of the power. This is the goal of all matching.
 shortReflected wave inverted. Total at load ✓. Current doubles.
 openReflected wave same polarity. Voltage doubles at the load; total current ✓.

(resistive)Partial same-polarity reflection.

Why for a pure reactance

. Numerator and denominator are complex conjugates of each other (up to sign: , and ). Equal magnitudes ⇒ , so : pure phase shift, no loss of amplitude.

Intuition — the rope analogy

Send a pulse down a light rope tied to a wall (a short: the end cannot move). The wall pushes back and the pulse returns upside down — . Tie the rope instead to a frictionless ring on a pole (an open end, free to move). The end overshoots and the pulse returns right way up — . Join the rope to another rope of exactly matched mass per length and nothing comes back at all — .

Impedance mismatch is the electrical version of a rope suddenly changing weight. Reflection is what an interface does when it cannot pass the wave through smoothly.

Passivity constraint

For any physically realisable passive load, , which forces . A reflection cannot come back bigger than it went out. On the complex -plane, all passive loads live inside the unit circle. (That circle is the outline of the Smith chart.)

The reflected wave travels back to the source. If , it reflects again there, with

and heads back to the load. And again. The pulse rattles back and forth, shrinking each round trip by a factor .

Derivation — the steady-state load voltage

Let be the initially launched wave. Accumulate everything that has arrived at the load as :

Geometric series with ratio (magnitude for passive terminations, so it converges):

Sanity check — it must equal the DC voltage divider. Substitute , :

Exactly the lumped voltage divider. ✓ The line has vanished from the answer.

Where the comes from — and why it is not part of the series

Careful bookkeeping. The waves travelling on the line and the voltage you would measure at the load are not the same thing.

Each time a wave of size arrives at the load, two waves exist there at once: the incident one, and the reflection it immediately creates, . A voltmeter at the load cannot separate them — it reads the sum:

So is the conversion from "size of the wave that arrived" to "voltage actually appearing across the load". It applies once to every arrival, so it factors straight out of the sum:

Two different roles, do not mix them up: converts wave amplitude into measured load voltage. counts up the infinitely many round trips.

Sanity-check it against things you already believe
  • Open circuit (): . The voltage doubles at an open end. The reflected wave arrives in phase and piles on top of the incident one. This is a real effect — it is how an unterminated cable can destroy an input.
  • Short circuit (): . The load voltage is zero — which it must be, because it is a short. The inverted reflection exactly cancels the incident wave.
  • Matched (): . No reflection, so what arrives is what you measure.

If your algebra ever produces a load voltage that does not satisfy these three, you have dropped or double-counted the .

The matching partner for current

Current has the opposite sign, because :

Check: at a short () the current factor is — current doubles, voltage vanishes. At an open () it is — no current, voltage doubles. Exactly swapped, as it should be.

Intuition

This is the punchline of the whole time-domain story: the transmission line only matters during the transient. Once the reflections have died out, the circuit settles into the boring answer you would have got from first-year circuit theory. The line's whole job is the first few nanoseconds — which is precisely when digital signal integrity lives or dies.

SECTION 7Sinusoidal steady state: phasors

Sections 4–6 followed a single pulse bouncing around. That works for a pulse. For a source that oscillates forever, waves are arriving and reflecting continuously and forever — tracking them one at a time is hopeless. Phasors solve the whole steady state in one shot.

Before you start

This section leans entirely on T4 in the Toolkit (spinning arrows, , and why becomes ). If that is hazy, read T4 first — the rest of this will be mechanical afterwards.

Step 1 — the observation that makes it all work

Drive a linear circuit with and something remarkable happens: every voltage and every current everywhere in it is also a cosine, at exactly the same frequency . Nothing can create a new frequency — only resistors, inductors and capacitors are present, and none of them can.

So at any point on the line, the voltage looks like

Read carefully what does and does not depend on position:

  • — the same everywhere. Carries no information about .
  • , the amplitude — varies with position.
  • , the phase — varies with position.
The insight

Only two numbers actually change as you move along the line: amplitude and phase. Everything else is fixed. So why drag the whole around in every equation? Track the two numbers that matter and throw away the rest.

Step 2 — pack those two numbers into one complex number

A complex number is a pair (length, angle). Perfect fit. Define

and to get the real signal back, multiply by the spinning part and take the horizontal shadow:

That formula, piece by piece
  • — a stationary arrow. Length , tilted at angle . This is the phasor. The tilde just means "this is a phasor, not a real signal."
  • — the spinner. Multiplying by it makes the arrow rotate at rad/s.
  • — "take the horizontal shadow." As the arrow spins, its shadow slides back and forth as a cosine.

Verify it does what we want:

The last step is Euler's formula: , so its real part is .

Now the trick

Every quantity in the circuit carries the same . It appears on both sides of every equation, so it can be cancelled from all of them. We simply stop writing it. From here on we work only with the stationary arrows and .

Nothing is lost. Whenever you want the real waveform back, reattach and take the real part.

Step 3 — why this is worth the trouble

The one property that does all the work

Differentiate a phasor signal with respect to time:

The survived untouched; the phasor just picked up a factor . Strip the spinner off both sides:

Step 4 — apply it to the telegrapher's equations

Recall them from Section 1:

"Hang on — how did vanish?"

It did not vanish. It cancelled. That is a completely different thing, and it is worth seeing the actual algebra rather than taking my word for it.

Start by writing both quantities in phasor form. Note carefully which variable each piece depends on:

depends on only. The exponential depends on only. The two variables have been separated into two separate factors — that is the whole manoeuvre.

Now substitute into telegrapher's equation (1), , and do each side separately.

Left side. We differentiate with respect to . The factor contains no , so it is a constant here and slides straight out:

Right side. We differentiate with respect to . Now it is that contains no , so it slides out, and the exponential differentiates to :

Set them equal, and look at what both sides have in common:

The same factor multiplies both sides. It is never zero, so divide it out:

And there is no left in the equation. Not because time stopped mattering — because time entered both sides in exactly the same way, so it carried no information.

The same idea without algebra

If , you conclude . You have not abolished the number 5; it was on both sides, so it told you nothing. is the 5.

Physically: every voltage and current in the circuit is whirling round at the same rate . Imagine stepping onto a carousel spinning at exactly that rate. Ride along, and none of the arrows appear to move at all — but the angles between them, which is the only thing that carries information, are completely unchanged.

The phasor domain is that rotating frame. Time still exists; you have just stopped describing the part of it that is common to everything.

So where is time kept?

In the recipe for getting it back. It was never lost:

Solve the -only equations, then reattach and take the real part whenever you want an actual waveform. Section 8 does exactly this to get the standing-wave patterns.

When you are NOT allowed to do this

The cancellation only works because every quantity shares one common . That requires two conditions:

  1. Linearity. Only , , — no diodes, nothing that could generate new frequencies. A second frequency would have a different exponential and nothing would cancel.
  2. Steady state. Transients must have died away. During the switch-on transient the waveform is not a pure sinusoid, so it cannot be written as a single phasor. That is precisely why Sections 4–6 had to be done in the time domain.

This is why the section is called sinusoidal steady state. The name is a statement of the two assumptions.

And why becomes

Purely notational, once you know what the symbols mean.

A curly says: "this function has several variables; differentiate with respect to this one and hold the others fixed." has two variables, so was the correct symbol — it meant "vary , freeze ."

But is a function of alone. There is nothing left to hold fixed, so the qualifier is redundant. A single-variable function takes an ordinary derivative, written .

SECTION 8Standing waves

A reflection means two waves now exist on the line at once, running in opposite directions. This section works out what their sum looks like — and the answer is strange enough that it gets its own name.

Step 1 — when two waves overlap, you just add them

Transmission lines are linear, so there is no interaction, no collision, no interference in the everyday sense. At each point the total voltage is simply the sum of whatever waves happen to be there:

That is the entire physics of this section. Everything below is just doing that sum carefully for one particular case.

Step 2 — the case to do first: a total reflection

Take an open-circuited line, so and the reflected wave is exactly as big as the incident one, . Write both waves out in the time domain:

(The sign inside the bracket is what sets the direction — see Section 2 if that is not automatic yet.)

Step 3 — do the sum

The algebra, with the identity spelled out

There is a standard trig identity for adding two cosines:

Here and . Work out the two brackets separately:

Substitute back, and use :

Step 4 — read what that result is telling you

Look at the shape of the answer, not the symbols

Compare the two forms side by side:

  • Travelling wave: .   and are locked together inside one bracket. Increase and you can undo it by increasing — which is exactly what "the shape slides along" means.
  • Our answer: .   and have separated into two independent factors. Nothing can slide.

That separation is the mathematical fingerprint of a standing wave. The factor fixes a shape in space, permanently. The factor just scales that whole shape up and down over time — like a rope being shaken, not like a wave rolling along it.

Watch it rather than read it

Standing waves are a motion phenomenon, so still pictures fight you. Press each of the four buttons below and watch what changes. Start with Matched to see what a normal travelling wave looks like, then go to Open and watch the motion stop dead.

Live standing-wave simulator — press a termination and watch
What to look for, in this order
  1. Matched (). One wave, marching steadily right. This is the normal case and the thing to compare everything else against.
  2. Open (). The bold curve stops travelling entirely. Fix your eye on a green dot: the curve is pinned to zero there permanently. Between the dots it just breathes up and down.
  3. Short (). Identical behaviour, but every node has shifted by . Same physics, different starting phase.
  4. Partial (). The honest general case, and the one exams use. It both drifts right and ripples in place. The dips no longer reach zero — and that non-zero minimum is exactly what VSWR measures in Section 9.

Turn off "the two waves" to see only what physically exists on the line. Turn it back on to see why.

If you prefer still frames, here is the same thing frozen at four instants through half a cycle:

The thing to actually notice

Follow one green dotted line down the four frames. At that position, the blue and red curves are always equal and opposite, so their sum is zero — at every instant, forever. It is not that the wave passes through zero there; it is that it is permanently pinned there.

Look at the third frame (): the entire line is momentarily flat. All the energy is in the current at that instant, none in the voltage. A quarter cycle later it will all be back in the voltage. The energy sloshes between the two rather than going anywhere.

Step 5 — where the nodes and antinodes are

Locating them

Nodes (permanently zero) occur wherever the spatial factor vanishes:

Antinodes (maximum swing) occur where it is :

Using to convert each time. The spacings that follow are worth memorising:

  • node to next node:
  • antinode to next antinode:
  • node to the neighbouring antinode:

Step 6 — the current does the opposite

Why sines appear instead of cosines

Voltage added because . But current has a minus sign (Section 3), so the two cosines subtract:

The companion identity is , and with the same two brackets as before:

The consequence — and it is a physical one

is zero exactly where peaks. So current nodes sit at voltage antinodes and vice versa, offset by all the way along.

Sanity check at the open end itself: an open circuit forces the current to zero there, and indeed at . Meanwhile , so the voltage is at a maximum. Exactly what an open circuit should do. ✓

Step 7 — why no power flows

Two separate reasons, both worth having

From the algebra: voltage goes as , current as . They are 90° out of phase in time, so the average of over a cycle is zero. No net power.

From common sense: the reflected wave is carrying away exactly as much power as the incident wave delivers, because nothing absorbs anything at an open circuit. Net transfer is zero by bookkeeping.

So a fully reflecting line is not a transmission system at all — it is a resonator. Energy shuttles between the electric field (piled up at voltage antinodes) and the magnetic field (at current antinodes) and never reaches the far end. Section 15 puts this to work deliberately.

Step 8 — the short-circuit case

For a short, , so and the two waves subtract instead. Running the identical algebra swaps the sines and cosines:

Same picture, nodes and antinodes swapped. Which is right: a short forces at , and . ✓

Exam

Given a termination, you should be able to say immediately where the first voltage node sits. Short → node at the load. Open → antinode at the load, first node back. Then everything repeats every . Sketching this correctly usually earns the marks even before any algebra.

Derivation

Two consequences, both enormous:

Consequence 1 — the magnitude never changes

Why physically: on a lossless line, power is dissipated only at the load. So the forward power and the backward power are each individually constant along the line, and their ratio must be constant. Only the phase relationship changes with position.

SECTION 12Open, short, and stubs

Set or in form (B). These "stubs" are the workhorses of microwave circuits.

Derivation

Shorted line, : numerator becomes , denominator :

Open line, : divide top and bottom by first, then let :

The product identity (an exam favourite):

Intuition — why they are purely imaginary

A lossless line with a lossless termination cannot dissipate anything. Whatever goes in comes back out. So the input impedance must be a pure reactance — a component that stores energy and gives it back. The line has become a capacitor or an inductor, depending only on its length.

This is the central microwave trick: at GHz frequencies you build inductors and capacitors out of lengths of copper, not out of components.

The length map — memorise this table

Length Shorted stub Open stub

→ inductive → capacitive
→ open → short
→ capacitive → inductive
Short (repeats)Open (repeats)
Intuition — why a short "becomes" an open at

Two ways to see it, both worth knowing:

Rotation: a short is , sitting on the far left of the -circle. Rotate (a move) and you land on : an open.

Standing wave: a short forces at the end — a voltage node. Nodes and antinodes alternate every . So a quarter wavelength back you are at a voltage antinode, which by the same argument is a current node. Voltage maximum with zero current means : an open. ✓

Practical payoff (your notes' last diagram): put a shorted stub across a line and it presents an open circuit — the signal is untouched. But at DC it is a dead short. So it is a mechanical support and a DC ground path that is invisible to the RF signal. Antenna masts genuinely work this way.

Frequency dependence — a trap

"" is only at one frequency. A fixed physical length has , which grows with frequency. Your notes' plot of versus frequency at fixed makes this point: the shorted stub is inductive, then resonant (open) at , then capacitive, then a short again at , and so on periodically. Every stub-based trick is inherently narrowband.

SECTION 13Power flow on the line

Derivation

Average power for phasors: . At the load:

The last bracket is of the form , so it contributes nothing to the real part:

Intuition

Delivered power = incident power − reflected power. Nothing more mysterious than that. The forward wave carries toward the load; a fraction of it bounces straight back.

Notice , not — power goes as amplitude squared. A "modest" reflects only 9% of the power. This is why VSWR 2 (, 11% reflected) is often considered acceptable.

Also: since is constant along a lossless line, is the same at every point. Energy is not accumulating anywhere. That is a good consistency check.

Exam

Related quantity you may meet: return loss dB. And "mismatch loss" dB. Both are just this formula in decibels.

Intuition

To first order, loss does not change how fast the wave goes or what impedance the line presents — it just makes the wave fade. splits cleanly into a conductor part () and a dielectric part (), so you can attribute attenuation to its physical cause.

Note also that is linear in , meaning all frequencies travel at the same speed — no dispersion, so pulse shapes survive. When the low-loss condition fails (as on long telegraph cables at low frequency) stops being linear, different frequencies travel at different speeds, and pulses smear into each other. That was the actual engineering crisis that produced this theory.

Notice what is not in the answer: length. depends only on the line's material quality, not how long you cut it. Making a resonator longer adds stored energy and loss in equal measure.

SECTION 16Quarter-wave impedance matching

The payoff. You have a source designed for (say 50 Ω) and a load that is not 50 Ω. Reflections waste power. Fix it with a single length of the right cable.

Derivation

Insert a section of line with its own characteristic impedance between the main line and the load. From Section 11, a quarter-wave line transforms:

For no reflection on the main line we need :

Intuition — why the geometric mean

The line inverts normalised impedance. Normalised to its own , the load looks like ; after inversion it looks like ; de-normalising gives . Setting that equal to says the transformer must sit exactly "halfway" between and — but multiplicatively, i.e. the geometric mean, because impedance transformation here is a multiplication, not an addition.

Analogy: it is the optical anti-reflection coating. To stop light reflecting between glass () and air () you coat with a quarter-wavelength layer of index . Identical mathematics, identical reason.

Two limitations you should state in an answer
  1. Narrowband. The section is only at the design frequency. Move off it and , the transformation is wrong, and reflections return. (Broadband versions use several cascaded sections.)
  2. Real loads only. needs real, or comes out complex, which no passive line can have. For a complex your notes give the standard fix: move back along the line to a point where the impedance is real (there is one every — at each voltage maximum and each minimum), and put the transformer there.

SECTION 19Traps, sign conventions and sanity checks

The seven ways to lose marks
  1. Direction of . is measured from the load, backwards toward the generator. Getting this backwards flips the sign in and rotates you the wrong way.
  2. The minus sign in . . Nearly every derivation depends on it.
  3. Radians, not degrees. goes into as radians.
  4. and are per unit length. Units H/m and F/m. Multiply by before using them as lumped values (e.g. in the derivation).
  5. Choosing the branch of . When solving something, there are infinitely many roots. Use the physics (inductive vs capacitive, shortest length) to pick.
  6. for power, for voltage.
  7. . Always pick the decaying root of .
Sanity checks to run on any answer
  • Is ? If not, you have made an algebra error (or the load is active).
  • Is VSWR ? Always.
  • For a lossless line with a lossless termination (open/short/pure reactance), is purely imaginary? It must be.
  • Does the transient answer converge to the DC voltage divider ?
  • Does return to when ? Good check on your .
  • Does the matched case () give , VSWR , for all ? Every general formula must collapse to this.
One mental model to carry into the exam

Everything in this course is one story told four ways:

Time domain: a pulse travels, hits a mismatch, part bounces back.
Frequency domain: forward and backward phasors interfere into a standing wave.
Impedance: the line transforms into as you walk away from it.
Geometry: rotates clockwise on a circle of fixed radius, one full turn per .

They are the same fact. If a question feels hard in one language, translate it into another. Most "hard" transmission-line problems are easy in the -circle picture.
